solution:
A had photographed a murder committed by B’s parent and reported it. The arrest forced B to move away to live with relatives. A felt guilty.
A’s surname later changed after parental divorce and remarriage. At university, A recognized B, but B did not recognize A. They genuinely fell in love and married.
Years later, B recognized A as the former classmate. B mistakenly believed A had not recognized B and did not know about B’s criminal parent. Ashamed and afraid of rejection, B disappeared, leaving divorce papers and an apology. B never learned that A had reported the crime.
Unable to find B, A fabricated evidence and falsely confessed to murdering B. A hoped the news would reach B, communicate acceptance of B’s past, and persuade B to return to clear A’s name. B was alive.
canonical_facts: A photographed and reported a murder by B’s parent; the arrest caused B to move away and A felt guilty
A’s surname changed after parental divorce and remarriage
At university A recognized B but B did not recognize A; they genuinely fell in love and married
B later recognized A, mistakenly believed A did not know the family history, and feared rejection
B voluntarily disappeared alive, leaving divorce papers and an apology, and never learned that A had reported the crime
A fabricated evidence and confessed falsely to killing B to reach B through the news
A hopes to communicate acceptance and make B return to clear A’s name
explicit_negatives: B is alive; the murder confession is false.
B never learns A reported the crime; this cannot be B’s reason for departure.
A recognizes B at university, while B initially does not recognize A.
unknown_details: Whether B ultimately returns and the eventual legal outcome are unspecified.
irrelevant_details: Unspecified names, exact dates, object brands and colors are incidental.

knowledge_states: At university A recognizes B and knows B’s criminal family past; B initially does not recognize A.
After marriage B recognizes A as a former classmate. B mistakenly thinks A does not know the family’s criminal past.
B does not discover that A witnessed/photographed/reported the murder as the trigger for leaving.
B remains alive. A’s confession is false and is intended to reach B through the news. Whether B eventually returns is unspecified.
label_boundaries: Recognition of an old classmate is not discovery of the informer’s identity.
No newly introduced deceased third-party association explains the disappearance. Reject that invented causal branch.

Separate intentional reporting from intent to make B transfer. B leaves and leaves divorce papers; broadly hiding the family secret or escaping its feared relationship consequences can describe B’s motive even though A already knows. Unknown witness status and when B first learned the crime are not additional facts.
